Cardiovascular.q: Can you explain “splitting of S2”? What does that even mean?
Cardiovascular.a: the aortic valve normally shuts (A2) just before the pulmonic valve (P2), so A2 will occur slightly before P2 = w hen we talk about changes in splitting of the S2 heart sound (i.e., wide splitting, paradoxical splitting, etc.), if pressure in a ventricle is greater, the sound will occur later / is protracted. So if RV pressure becomes greater for whatever reason = P2 occurs later = wider splitting. So pulmonary artery hypertension = wide

Cardiovascular.a: Increased venodilatio n + venous pooling = decreased venous return to the right heart = decreased cardiac preload.

Cardiovascular.q: “Wait, can you explain cor pulmonal e a little more. I’ve heard that a lot but don’t really understand it.”

Cardiovascular.q: How does isolat ed right heart failure present?
Cardiovascular.a: right ventricular hypertrophy (unless tricuspid pathology), jugular venous distension (JVD), peripheral edema, hepatosplenomegaly (late).

Cardiovascular.q: What’s the most common cause of right heart failure?
Cardiovascular.a: left heart failure.

Cardiovascular.a: right heart failure + left heart failure.

Cardiovascular.q: What causes left heart failure?
Cardiovascular.a: systemic HTN, ischemia (atherosclerosis), valvular abnormalities.

Cardiovascular.q: Since left heart failure is the most common cause of right heart failure, what usually causes isolated right heart failure?
Cardiovascular.a: lung pathology = when you have lung pathology causing RH failure, that’s called cor pulmonale.

Cardiovascular.q: year Hx of smoking + JVD + peripheral edema; Dx?
Cardiovascular.a: cor pulmonale = signs of RH failure in someone who has lung disease.

Cardiovascular.q: year Hx of smoking + systemic HTN + JVD + peripheral edema + has crackles in lungs + dilated heart on CXR ; Dx?
Cardiovascular.a: congestive heart failure; patient has combo of left and right heart failure signs.

Cardiovascular.q: 25M + cystic fibrosis + JVD + peripheral edema + crackles in lungs ; Dx ?
Cardiovascular.a: cor pulmonale = crackles due to CF, not LH failure.

Cardiovascular.q: If USMLE asks you for the mechanism of cor pulmonale, what’s the answer?
Cardiovascular.a: pulmonary hypertension = hypoxic vasoconstriction (e.g., in chronic bronchitis, CF) or obliteration of pulmonary parenchyma (emphysema) will cause a backup of blood and pulmonary HTN = increased afterload on RV = starts the process of cor pulmonale (mere pulmonary HTN is not cor pulmonale; there must be RH failure). Gastrointestinal.a: HNPCC (Lynch syndrome), not FAP = FAP has hundreds or thousands of polyps on colonoscopy; HNPCC has “some polyps.”

Gastrointestinal.q: 22F + has 30 polyps on colonoscopy + mom died of endometrial cancer; Dx?
Gastrointestinal.a: HNPCC = Lynch syndrome associated with gyn tumors such as ovarian + endometrial, as well as other organ system tumors such as pancreas, stomach, and small bowel. Testicular + prostate very r are, but gyn common.

Gastrointestinal.q: 42M + EtOH Hx + dysphagia to solids that progresses to include liquids; Dx?
Gastrointestinal.a: esophageal cancer (SCC) = dysphagia to solids that progresses to solids + liquids = cancer until proven otherwise.

Gastrointestinal.q: HY points about esophageal cance r?
Gastrointestinal.a: adenocarcinoma is distal 1/3 and is caused by GERD (obesity = low LES tone = GERD = Barrett = adenocarcinoma); SCC is upper 2/3 of esophagus and is caused by smoking + alcohol; can also be caused by webs, burns, chemicals, and achalasia (difficult, be cause achalasia is LES so your thought is, “how can that cause SCC of upper 2/3?” = probably the dysphagia causes increased esophageal irritation, which then becomes the risk factor for SCC).

Gastrointestinal.q: How do you Dx achalasia?
Gastrointestinal.a: US MLE wants barium (or gastrografin) swallow, then manometry, then confirmatory biopsy, in that order. There is a Q on an NBME for 2CK where both barium and manometry were listed, and the answer was barium swallow, not manometry.

Gastrointestinal.q: So when is manometry the answer for achalasia?
Gastrointestinal.a: when they show you a pic of the bird’s beak from the barium swallow already per formed, so clearly the next best step is manometry. The USMLE will sometimes show a graph of a manometry that’s been performed, and you’ll simply see that the pressure is high at the LES = hence Dx = achalasia. The confirmatory / most accurate test is biop sy of LES showing loss of neurons.

Gastrointestinal.q: 42M + overweight + halitosis + gurgling sound when drinking fluids + occasionally regurgitates undigested food; next best step in Mx?

Dysphagia is a risk factor because this increases oropharyngeal pressure. I’ve noticed Zenker vignettes often mention the patient is overweight, although the association is non

Gastrointestinal.q: MOA of ETEC HL toxin?
Gastrointestinal.a: HL toxin ADP ribosylates adenylyl cyclase = increases cAMP = increases Cl secretion into small bowel lumen = Na follows Cl = water follows Na = secretory diarrhea.

Gastrointestinal.q: Which organism has same MOA as ETEC HL toxin?
Gastrointestinal.a: Cholera toxin = difference is cholera is described as “liters and liters” of high

Gastrointestinal.q: MOA of ETEC HS toxin?
Gastrointestinal.a: ADP ribosylates guanylyl cyclase = increases cGMP = decreases Cl reabsorption from lumen = more Na stays in lumen = more water stays with Na = watery diarrhea.

Gastrointestinal.q: Which organism has same MOA as E TEC HS toxin?
Gastrointestinal.a: Yersinia enterocolitica toxin = difference is Y. enterocolitica causes bloody, not watery, diarrhea, and Y. enterocolitica also causes pseudoappendicitis in children (due to terminal ileitis / mesenteric adenitis) and arthritis in adults.

Gastrointestinal.q: R eheated fried rice + watery diarrhea; organism + mechanism?

Gastrointestinal.q: Kid + bloody diarrhea + petechiae + red urine; Dx?

Gastrointestinal.q: How does HUS contrast with TTP?
Gastrointestinal.a: TTP is caused by a mutation that results in defective ADAMTS13, or antibodies against ADAMTS13, resulting in the inability to cleave vWF multimers = platelet clumping = similar progression as HUS. One of the points of contrast is that TTP is not toxin

Gastrointestinal.a: true = contains all layers of bowel = mucosa + submucosa + muscularis propria + adventitia; in contrast, false (Zenker) is just mucosa + submucosa.

Hematology & Oncology.a: = thalassemia. Presents as a microcytic anemia despite a normal iron and ferritin.

Hematology & Oncology.a: = anemia of chronic disease (AoCD). In contrast, IDA you'll have low iron + low ferritin ; t halassemia you'll have normal iron + normal ferritin. Also, for AoCD, there will be obvious cause like renal failure, autoimmune disease, cancer, or chronic infection like hepatitis B/C.

Hematology & Oncology.q: 32F + low MCV + low Hb + high transferrin binding capacity; Dx?

Hematology & Oncology.q: 32F + low MCV + low Hb + no improvement with iron supplementation; Dx + next best step in Mx?

Hematology & Oncology.a: decreased production of one type of hemoglobin chain (i.e., if ¯ alpha chain production, then Dx is alpha thalassemia; same for beta, respectively ).

Hematology & Oncology.q: 32F + pregnant + completely asymptomatic till this point + low MCV + low Hb + starts taking prenatal vitamin supplement + three weeks later still has low MCV and low Hb; next best step?
Hematology & Oncology.a: = hemoglobin electrophoresis. Dx = thalassemia.

Neurology.q: How to Mx carotid plaques?
Neurology.a: first we have to ask whether the patient is symptomatic or asymptomatic. A bruit does not count as symptoms (that's a sign). Symptomatic means stroke, TIA, or retinal artery occlusion . According to recent guidelines: c arotid occlusion >70% if symptomatic, or >80% if asymptomatic = = do carotid endarterectomy. Below these thresholds = = medical management = statin, PLUS clopidogrel OR dipyridamole + aspirin. The U SMLE will actually

Neurology.a: superior temporal gyrus ( temporal lobe ).

Neurology.q: What is conduction aphasia?
Neurology.a: patient has only impaired repetition (arcuate fasciculus connecting Broca and Wernicke areas).

Neurology.q: What is global aphasia?
Neurology.a: patient has presentation of Broca and Wernicke aphasias at the same time.

Neurology.q: What is transcortical motor aphasia?
Neurology.a: patient sounds like he/she has Broca aphasia but repetition is intact.

Neurology.q: What is transcortic al sensory aphasia?
Neurology.a: patient sounds like he/she has Wernicke aphasia but repetition is intact.

Neurology.q: What is mixed transcortical aphasia?
Neurology.a: patient sounds like he/she has Broca and Wernicke at the same time but repetition is intact.

Neurology.q: right agnosia + finger agnosia + agraphia; Dx?

Neurology.q: Lacunar infarct HY points?
Neurology.a: caused by HTN leading to lipohyalinosis of lenticulostriate vessels = if affecting posterior limb of internal capsule, deficits are pure motor (contralateral); if thalamic, deficits are pure sensory (contralateral).

Neurology.q: Correct hypernatremia too quickly?

Neurology.q: Pain in contralateral limb months after stroke resolves; Dx?
Neurology.a: thalamic pain syndrome.

Neurology.q: Coma or persistent vegetative state following deceleration injury (i.e., MVA or fall); Dx?

Psychiatry.a: anticholinergic effects of TCA.

Psychiatry.a: Creutzfeldt

Psychiatry.a: = prog ressive supranuclear palsy (student had this on the USMLE).

Psychiatry.a: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors first (donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine); sometimes Q will ask for mechanism, and = “cholinergic”; for more advanced disease try NMDA (glutamate) receptor antagonist (memantine).

Psychiatry.q: 74M + MMSE 22/30 + avoids eye contact + weight loss + low mood; DX and Tx?
Psychiatry.a: pseudodementia = Tx = sertraline (SSRI), not donepezil.

Psychiatry.q: Main way to differ entiate pseudodementia from dementia?
Psychiatry.a: pseudodementia is depression that presents as cognitive decline; vignette may describe weight loss or gain , avoidance of eye contact, low mood, and/or tearing up during interview; vignette may also mention poor perfo rmance on the reverse serial 7s of the MMSE, or the patient is slow drawing a clockface but can rapidly complete it once prompted (apathy); pseudodementia presents as apathy on MMSE; in contrast, patients with true dementia try on the MMSE.

Psychiatry.q: How to differen tiate normal aging from Alzheimer on Psych shelf?
Psychiatry.a: biggest point is that patients who complain or are concerned about their own cognitive decline do not have Alzheimer; classic example is 68F who frequently says she walks into rooms and can’t remember why she went in there + says she accidentally left the burner on in the kitchen last week and had an argument with her adult daughter about it = = normal aging, not dementia = patient herself is concerned / complaining, so answer is not dementia on USM LE.

Psychiatry.q: Other notable causes of reversible cognitive decline?
Psychiatry.a: hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, neuro Lyme.

Psychiatry.q: 53M + BMI 25 + mostly quiet during interview + total cholesterol 300 mg/dL + hepatic AST slightly elevated + HR 60; Dx + next best step i n Mx + Tx?
Psychiatry.a: hypothyroidism = check serum TSH = give levothyroxine (T4); hypothyroidism can cause dysthymia, high cholesterol, and elevated hepatic transaminases.

Psychiatry.q: 48F + BMI 26 + cholesterol elevated + HR 55 + creatine kinase (CK) elevated; Dx?
Psychiatry.a: hypothyroidism = check serum TSH; hypothyroid myopathy ca n cause proximal muscle weakness + elevated serum CK.

Psychiatry.q: acute neurologic findings; next best step?
Psychiatry.a: assess suicide risk (this answer is basically always correct if it’s listed).

Psychiatry.q: acute neurologic findings + MMSE is 25/30 + no suicidal ideation; next best step?
Psychiatry.a: check serum B12 = subacute combined degeneration (SCD) = pattern of neurologic dysfunction s een in B12 deficiency.

Psychiatry.q: Which three spinal tracts are involved in SCD?
Psychiatry.a: lateral corticospinal, spinocerebellar, dorsal columns = just remember that the spinothalamic is not involved.

Psychiatry.q: 68M + started on various medications 8 weeks ago for low ejection fractio n heart failure + now has depressed mood; most likely cause?

Psychiatry.q: What is cyclothymia vs dysthymia?
Psychiatry.a: cyclothymia is >2 years of swinging low + elevated moods, but never meets the thresholds for bipolar + never has true depressive episode. Dysthymia is >2 years of low moods not ever meeting thresholds for MDD.

Psychiatry.a: Psych NBME wants lorazepam, not propranolol (because asthma patient). o 27M + very anxious about speech he needs to make soon; Tx? = Psych NBME wants propranolol, not lorazepam .

Psychiatry.a: neuroleptic malignant syndrome; give dantrolene (inhibits ryanodine channel).

Psychiatry.a: akathisia; Tx with propra nolol. Psych shelf has Q where patient says: “I feel as though I am going to jump out of my skin!” = = “adverse effect of prochlorperazine.”

Psychiatry.q: A ntipsychotic med + abnormal tongue movements; Dx + Tx?
Psychiatry.a: tardive dyskinesia; stop antipsychotic + switch to atypical = answer on Psych shelf for one Q is “discontinue haloperidol and switch to risperidone.”

Psychiatry.q: Mechanism for tardive dyskinesia?
Psychiatry.a: answer on Psy ch NBME = “increased sensitivity of dopamine receptors.”

Psychiatry.a: answ er on Psych NBME = fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), not Down syndrome; everyone says wtf about this question, so what I tell my students is: if Q sounds like Down syndrome but they mention anything about the philtrum (i.e., long, smooth, indistinct, etc.), the answer is FAS, not Down.

Psychiatry.q: 6M + IQ of 60 + small for age + born to female age 41 + no other information given; Q asks: most likely cause of mental retardation?
Psychiatry.a: = Down syndrome, not FAS; although FAS is most common cause of MR overall, two points: 1) if they want FAS, they’ll mention the philtrum as per above, and 2) most common cause of MR over the age of 40 is Down, not FAS.

Psychiatry.q: 8M + prominent jaw + protruding ears + IQ of 65; most likely explanation?
Psychiatry.a: “Fragile site on the X chro mosome” = Fragile X (CGG TNR disorder).

Psychiatry.q: 7M + prominent ears + flattened nasal bridge + long philtrum + low IQ; Dx?
Psychiatry.a: FAS, not Fragile X; the Q mentions the philtrum.

Psychiatry.q: 4F + wringing of the hands + putting objects in her mouth + less eye contact; Dx?

Renal.a: aka interstitial nephritis, or tubulointerstitial nephritis, where there are WBCs (eosinophils) in the urin e; patient may or may not present with a fine maculopapular rash = almost always due to beta

Renal.q: 62M + 6 weeks nafcillin for MSSA endocarditis + WBCs on U/A ; Dx?
Renal.a: interstitial nephropathy.

Renal.q: 35F + uses ibuprofen daily for headaches + rash + eosinophils in urine; what do you see on biopsy?
Renal.a: NBME an swer = “inflammatory infiltrates in the interstitium” = interstitial nephropathy.

Renal.q: What is analgesic nephropathy?
Renal.a: renal damage due to NSAIDs = can be renal papillary necrosis, interstitial nephritis, or generalized edema from reduced renal blood flow. If renal papillary necrosis, will present with dark urine from ischemia. If interstitial nephritis, will present with eosinophils in urine as described previously (patient may not necessarily have a rash). Analgesic nephropathy is not a specific/different ren al diagnosis. It is just an umbrella term that refers to any situation in which the kidney is fucked up due to NSAIDs.

Renal.q: 80F + taking high doses of naproxen for 6 weeks for osteoarthritis + peripheral edema; mechanism of the edema?
Renal.a: Mechanism for edema in setting of NSAID use = USMLE = “ increased renal retention of sodium ,” or “ decreased renal excretion of sodium. ”

Renal.q: Why would analgesic nephropathy cause increased renal retention of sodium?
Renal.a: NSAID knocks out COX = decreased pro staglandin synthesis = decreased diameter of afferent arterioles = decreased

Renal.q: Patient with analgesic nephropathy; USMLE Q asks mechanism in terms of NSAID’s ability to inhibit constriction/dilation at afferent vs efferent arterioles;
Renal.a: “vasodilating prostaglandins at afferent arteriole ,” caus ing reduced renal blood flow.

Renal.q: When is renal papillary necrosis the answer?
Renal.a: classically in sickle cell; can also from drugs like NSAIDs; urine will be dark = renal papillae in the medulla receive less blood flow, so small changes in the microvascular supp ly can lead to sloughing + necrosis of the medulla. You’ll be able to contrast this disorder from diffuse cortical necrosis and acute tubular necrosis because the latter two conditions, in the context of ischemia, are associated with massive, acute events.

Renal.q: Tx for calcium oxalate stones?
Renal.a: fluids, then alkalinize urine (citrate); prevent recurrence with thiazide (decrease urinary Ca).

Renal.q: Tx for calcium phosphate stones?
Renal.a: fluids; prevent recurrence with thiazide (decrease urinary Ca). Calcium phosphate stones form at higher pH, so do not alkalinize; CaOxalate stones form at lower pH, which is why citrate helps.

Renal.q: Tx for struvite (ammonium magnesium phosphate) stones?
Renal.a: fluid s; acidify urine with ammonium chloride; surgery (because they’re often huge).

Renal.q: Tx for uric acid stones?
Renal.a: fluids + alkalinize urine with citrate; treat the underlying gout; avoid uricosurics such as probenecid indefinitely; avoid low

Renal.q: Tx for c ystine stones?
Renal.a: fluids; alkalinize urine with citrate.

Renal.q: Who gets calcium oxalate stones?
Renal.a: classically those with intestinal malabsorptive disorders such as Crohn, Celiac, CF = malabsorption of fats means increased intraintestinal binding of fat to calcium = less calcium available to bind oxalate intraluminally = more oxalate is absorbed throug h intestinal wall. CaOxalate stones can also be seen in ethylene glycol (AntiFreeze) poisoning and hypervitaminosis C.

Renal.q: Who gets struvite stones?
Renal.a: UTIs caused by urease (+) organisms. Proteus spp. is classic. Stones are coffin lid

Renal.q: Who gets uric aci d stones?
Renal.a: generally uric acid over

Renal.q: Who get cystine stones?
Renal.a: patients with cystinuria caused by inability to absorb COLA (cysteine, ornithine, lysine, arginine) = two cysteines (

Renal.q: Any factoid to know about cystine stones?
Renal.a: AR disorder; generally young adults in USMLE vignette; nitroprusside urine test yields a magenta color; hexagon

Renal.q: What do I need to know about renal tubular acidosis type I (RTA I)?
Renal.a: decreased ability of the DCT to secrete protons (urine pH i s >5.5) = leads to metabolic acidosis; patient does not have hyperkalemia. Can be associated with bilateral renal parenchymal stones (i.e., not within the lumina but instead in the actual meat of the kidney); can be seen in Sjogren syndrome.

Renal.q: What do I nee d to know about renal tubular acidosis type II (RTA II)?
Renal.a: decreased ability of the PCT to reabsorb bicarb (urine pH is >5.5) = associated with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and Fanconi syndrome (expired tetracyclines). Patient does not have hyperkalemia.

Renal.q: What do I need to know about renal tubular acidosis type IV (RTA IV)?
Renal.a: either hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone insensitivity at the kidney (urine pH <5.5) = patient will present with lab values resembling Addison disease, but the etiology will be chronic renal failure, not adrenal. For instance, 68F diabetic with biochemistry resembling Addison = RTA IV, not Addison = patient will have low serum sodium, high potassium, low bicarb (metabolic acidosis). Patient is hyperkalemic, in contrast to RTA I and II.

Renal.q: USMLE Q asks “decreased absorption” vs “no change” for Fanconi syndrome with respect to glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarb
Renal.a: = decreased absorptio n for all four.

Renal.q: Where does aldosterone act in the kidney?
Renal.a: cortical collecting duct; binds to intracytosolic receptor, causing upregulation of basolateral Na/K

Renal.q: Another important point about renin secretion?
Renal.a: USMLE wants you to know that beta

Renal.q: Where does vasopressin (ADH) act in the kidney?
Renal.a: medullary collecting duct = inserts aquaporins on apical membrane = increased free water reabsorption.

Renal.q: Four causes of nephrogenic DI or USMLE ?
Renal.a: lithium + demeclocycline are the two highest yield . NSAIDs and hypercalcemia can also cause it.

Renal.q: What is the macula densa?
Renal.a: modified smooth muscle cells of the DCT that sense changes in serum sodium, thereby triggering the JGC to secrete renin; if volume status is low, PCT is attempting to reabsorb more water to compensate; in order to do so, it reabsorbs more Na, where water follows Na. This means that less sodi um will still be left in the urine in the DCT . The macula densa will sense

Renal.q: What do I need to know about mannitol?
Renal.a: osmotic diuretic tha t acts by retaining water within the nephron lumina; USMLE likes proximal straight tubule (short segment after the PCT) as the answer if it shows you a drawing and is very specific; if proximal straight tubule isn’t shown or labeled, choose thin descending limb over PCT. Avoid in heart failure because administration transiently increases intravascular volume = increased preload going to RA = increased myocardial oxygen demand. Mannitol is used to treat increased intracranial pressure (pseudotumor cerebri) i n some patients after intubation + hyperventilation have been instituted (decreased CO2 = decreased cerebral perfusion).

Renal.q: What do I need to know about acetazolamide and the kidney?
Renal.a: carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that acts to prevent bicarb reabsorption = ca uses a transient metabolic acidosis that can be used to counteract the respiratory alkalosis secondary to altitude sickness (kidney cannot physiologically compensate fast enough so the drug forces the metabolic acidosis).

Renal.q: What do I need to know about Loops ?
Renal.a: Furosemide is standard first

Renal.q: How are calcium + magnesium reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb?
Renal.a: paracellular (between the cells).

Renal.q: What is Bartter syndrome?
Renal.a: disease that presents as though the patient is indefinitely on loop diuretic (associated with JGC hyperplasia).

Renal.q: What do I need to know about thiazides?
Renal.a: hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) is standard drug = inhibits the Na/Cl symporter on the apical membrane of the early

Renal.q: What is Gitelman syndrome?
Renal.a: disease that presents as though the patient is indefinitely on thiazide diuretic.

Renal.q: What do I need to know about amiloride and triamterene?
Renal.a: simply that they’re ENaC inhibitors and are potassium

Renal.q: What do I need to know about spironolactone?
Renal.a: aldosterone receptor antagonist used in heart failure after the patient is already on ACEi (or ARB) and a beta

Renal.q: What do I need to know abou t tolvaptan/conivaptan?
Renal.a: vasopressin (ADH) receptor antagonists that can be used in SIADH (e.g., due to small cell lung cancer).

Renal.q: “I don’t get it though. If vi tamin D deficiency is associated with decreased Ca + decreased PO4, and there’s vitamin D deficiency in chronic renal failure, why are the electrolytes in CRF decreased Ca + increased PO4?”
Renal.a: answer is: the renal disease always wins; yes, there’s decreased PO4 absorption in the small bowel, but there’s also decreased filtration at the kidney, and the latter wins in terms of the arrows. That is: o Vitamin D deficiency due to renal failure: low Ca + high PO4. o Vitamin D deficiency not due to renal failure: low Ca + low PO4.

Renal.q: related pathology is seen in renal disease?
Renal.a: secondary hyperparathyroidism is caused by chronic renal failure = kidney cannot reabsorb Ca in the DCT or synthesis 1,25

Renal.q: D3; USMLE asks about 24,25 sometimes). Student then asks, “I don’t get it though. If vi tamin D deficiency is associated with decreased Ca + decreased PO4, and there’s vitamin D deficiency in chronic renal failure, why are the electrolytes in CRF decreased Ca + increased PO4?”
Renal.a: answer is: the renal disease always wins; yes, there’s decreased PO4 absorption in the small bowel, but there’s also decreased filtration at the kidney, and the latter wins in terms of the arrows. That is: o Vitamin D deficiency due to renal failure: low Ca + high PO4. o Vitamin D deficiency not due to renal failure: low Ca + low PO4.

Renal.q: What is renal osteodystrophy?
Renal.a: any bone problem caused by renal disease , but is usually synonymous with “renal

Renal.q: Patient with chronic renal disease has a pseudo fracture of the hip; Dx?
Renal.a: osteomalacia = “pseudofracture” is pathognomonic for vitamin D deficiency; in this case, the pseudofracture is just a type of renal osteodystrophy that may be seen.

Renal.q: Patient has renal failure + friction rub heard on auscultation o f the chest; Dx + Tx?
Renal.a: uremic pericarditis (a type of fibrinous pericarditis) = USMLE Tx is immediate hemodialysis.

Renal.q: base disturbance seen in renal disease?
Renal.a: sodium is variable; potassium high; calcium low; phosphate high; b icarb low; pH low; CO2 low (compensation).

Renal.q: What do I need to know about EPO and the kidney?
Renal.a: Kidney secretes it in response to anemia / low oxygen states (e.g., COPD). EPO deficiency occurs in renal failure, leading to anemia of chronic disease. EPO exces s secretion can occur in renal cell carcinoma.

Renal.q: Smoker + hypercalcemia + polycythemia + hematuria ; Dx?
Renal.a: RCC (paraneoplastic EPO + PTHrp).

Renal.q: Most common type of RCC?
Renal.a: clear cell carcinoma (histo shows large clear cells on Step 1).

Renal.q: Renal cancer in children?
Renal.a: Wilms tumor.

Renal.q: 3M + painless flank mass + no other info; Dx?
Renal.a: Wilms tumor.

Renal.q: 6M + painless flank mass + seizure + MRI of brain shows periventricular nodules; Dx?
Renal.a: Tuberous sclerosis with renal angiomyolipoma.

Renal.q: Anything else about Wilms tumor?
Renal.a: increased incidence in horseshoe kidney in Turner syndrome.

Renal.q: Horseshoe kidney key point?
Renal.a: not only increased risk of Wilms tumor, but the kidney gets caught under the IMA.

Renal.q: What is WAGR complex?
Renal.a: Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary malformation, Retardation; caused by WT1 gene mutation.

Renal.q: renal location for cysts in A DPKD?
Renal.a: liver.

Renal.q: What’s more important in management of ADPKD, serial BP checks or MRI angiogram circle of Willis?
Renal.a: = serial BP checks = renal cysts compress microvasculature, causing surges in RAAS.

Renal.q: Comment on systemic sclerosis and the kidney?
Renal.a: sy stemic sclerosis (diffuse type) can cause renal crises with malignant HTN.

Renal.q: 68M + diabetic + Hx of intermittent claudication + CABG + gradually increasing BP past two years; Dx?
Renal.a: renal artery stenosis.

Renal.q: Cause of renal artery stenosis?
Renal.a: atherosclerosis. The y will always give RAS in a patient who has cardiovascular disease.

Renal.q: 23F + high aldosterone + high renin + high BP; Dx?
Renal.a: fibromuscular dysplasia = this is not renal artery stenosis; if you say RAS, that means atherosclerosis. FMD is a tunica media prolifer ative pathology resulting in RAS

Renal.q: Patient with high BP is given an ACEi or ARB and gets a spike in either renin or creatinine; Dx?
Renal.a: FMD if young patient; RAS if patient with CVD. USMLE loves this point and it shows up on Steps 1 and 2CK. If you have FMD or RA S, renal blood flow is already reduced, so the kidney has a reduced capacity to remain within physiologic range for GFR = giving an ACEi or ARB will reduce filtration fraction and lead to a clinically significant reduction in GFR = renin + Cr go up.

Renal.q: What is Brenner tumor?
Renal.a: ovarian tumor with bladder (transitional cell) epithelium.

Renal.q: Is chronic pyelonephritis ever an answer?
Renal.a: usually young patient, i.e., 3

Renal.q: Q asks best initial Mx to prevent UTIs
Renal.a: = postcoital voiding. If unsuccessful, NBME wants “postcoital nitrofurantoin prophylaxis” next; if not listed, choose “daily TMP/SMX prophylaxis.” The latter sounds incredibly wrong, and I agree, sounds outrageous, but it’s correct on one of the obgyn CMS forms and everyone gets it wrong.

Renal.q: 22F + Sx of dysuria for 6 months + anterior vaginal wall pain + U/A completely normal + afebrile; Dx?
Renal.a: chronic interstitial cystitis = answer on one of the obgyn forms. Must have at least 6 weeks of UTI

Renal.q: Why must Tx asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy?
Renal.a: progesterone slows ureteric peristalsis, increasing the risk of pyelo.

Renal.q: 4 RBCs/hpf on LM; Dx?
Renal.a: rhabdomyolysis = need to know that false (+) blood on urine dipstick is rhabdomyolysis (dipstick cann ot differentiate myoglobinuria from actual RBCs).

Renal.q: 22F has Sx of UTI + U/A completely normal; next best step?
Renal.a: test for chlamydia/gonorrhea (answer on one of the newer obgyn forms).

Renal.q: 25M + mucopurulent urethral discharge + culture grows nothing; Dx?
Renal.a: chlam ydia (obligate intracellular).

Renal.q: Most common type of bladder cancer?
Renal.a: transitional cell carcinoma.

Renal.q: Most specific cause of bladder cancer?
Renal.a: industrial (aniline) dyes.

Renal.q: Most common cause of bladder cancer?
Renal.a: smoking.

Renal.q: What is Potter s equence?
Renal.a: renal agenesis leading to oligohydramnios = causes pulmonary hypoplasia in fetus.

Renal.q: Most common genitourinary (GU) abnormality in neonatal males?
Renal.a: posterior urethral valves (PUV) = thin membrane(s) in the urethra preventing the outflow of urine .

Renal.q: Neonatal male with PUV; next best step in Dx?
Renal.a: ultrasound then voiding cystourethrogram.

Renal.q: 34M falls on balance beam + saddle injury + blood at urethral meatus; Dx + next best step in Mx?
Renal.a: ur ethral injury; do retrograde urethrogram.

Renal.q: 16M + skiing accident + bruising and/or pain over a flank + red urine; Dx + next best step in Mx?
Renal.a: kidney injury; must do CT with contrast, not ultrasound. This is exceedingly HY on surgery forms and sounds wrong (i.e., “why would you do CT with contrast in someone with suspected renal injury if

Renal.q: MEHLMANMEDICAL.COM MEHLMANMEDICAL.COM 49 contrast can cause nephrotoxicity?”)
Renal.a: great question, but CMS/NBME/USMLE still want CT with contrast, so don’t pick ultrasound.

Renal.q: 16M + skiing accident + bruising and/or pa in over a flank + no gross blood of urine (i.e, urine not red); next best step in Mx?
Renal.a: urinalysis to look for blood (super HY) = if urinalysis shows blood, do CT scan to check for renal injury. If U/A negative, renal injury unlikely, so choose “no further investigations indicated,” not CT.

Renal.q: 16M + skiing accident + bruising and/or pain over a flank + urinalysis is normal; next best step?
Renal.a: no further investigations indicated.

Renal.q: USMLE Q gives you creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL in 65M, then tells you 10 years later his Cr is 1.2 mg/dL; Dx?
Renal.a: normal aging = creatinine clearance naturally decreases with age. There is no definitive cutoff for USMLE Qs, but the student should be aware that Cr of 1.5 or greater is always pathologic, and at Cr of 2.0, >90% of nephron function has already been lost. Normal range is 0.7

Renal.q: USMLE Q says oophorectomy is being performed + ureter is damaged; during ligation of which vessel did the damage to the ureter occur?
Renal.a: = ovarian artery.

Renal.q: What is water under the bridge?
Renal.a: ureter travels under the uterine artery in women and vas defe rens in men.

Renal.q: Kid + bloody diarrhea + petechiae + red urine; Dx?
Renal.a: hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) caused by EHEC O157:H7 or Shigella = HUS = triad of thrombocytopenia + schistocytosis (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia) + renal insufficiency .

Renal.q: How does HUS contrast with TTP?
Renal.a: TTP is caused by a mutation that results in defective ADAMTS13, or antibodies against ADAMTS13, resulting in the inability to cleave vWF multimers = platelet clumping = similar progression as HUS. One of the points of contrast is that TTP is not toxin

Renal.q: What is hepatorenal syndrome?
Renal.a: liver failure causing renal failure; rare Dx but the correct answer USMLE wants is “normal renal biopsy.”

Renal.q: Endocardit is following a genitourinary procedure (e.g., TURP) or catheterization; organism?
Renal.a: USMLE wants enterococcus.

Reproductive.q: USMLE will ask, “If an episiotomy is performed posteriorly in the midline and the doctor cuts too far, what will he/she cut into?”

Reproductive.q: binding globulin (TBG) production by the liver. TBG is the protein carrier molecule for thyroid hormone in the blood. An NBME Q asks for which hormone causes the TBG in pregnancy
Reproductive.a: = estrogen, not progesterone.

Reproductive.a: = ampicillin + gentamicin; vancomycin + ceftriaxone is wrong on the form.

Reproductive.a: L shunt across the foramen ovale. Student says, “Wait, but isn’t the foramen ovale between the atria, and that’s only open in the fetus but is supposed to close after birth?” Correct. Hence we have persistent fetal circulation.

Reproductive.a: = adenomyosis. Student is confused and says “how can she be pregnant if she had tubule ligation?” She’s not. Use your head. It’s just how the Q can describe the uterine size.

Reproductive.q: “What do I need to know about which bodily structures/organs originating from certain germ layers, i.e., ectoderm, etc.?” o Most embryologic derivative memorization is nonsense, especially now that Step 1 is P/F. o A good rule of thumb is: if you literally have no idea on a USMLE question what the answer is, neural crest is usually correct. I’d say this is the case in at least 3/4 of questions. o “Failure of neural crest migration” is answer for heart defects due to DiGeorge syndrome and fetal alcohol syndrome. It’s also answer for Hirschsprung disease. o Additionally, you sh ould be aware that pheochromocytoma, melanoma, and neurofibromatosis I/II are neural crest. o Craniopharyngioma = derived from Rathke pouch, which is the “roof of the primitive pharynx”; considered ectoderm. o Thyroglossal duct cyst = derived from “endoderm of foramen cecum”; the latter is the base of the tongue; in other words, the thyroid gland starts off embryologically at base of tongue and descends. o CAP = Clefts, Arches, Pouches; clefts (aka grooves) become ectoderm; arches become mesoderm; pouches become endoderm. o Ectoderm
Reproductive.a: highest

Reproductive.q: “Which organ is supplied by an artery of the foregut but is not itself derived from the foregut”
Reproductive.a: answer = spleen; supplied by Celiac trunk but derived from midgut).

Reproductive.q: “atrialization of right ventricle”
Reproductive.a: the right ventricle is tiny and right atrium massive). o Anti

Reproductive.q: “What do I need to know about Mullerian vs Wolffian duct stuff, etc.?” o Mullerian (paramesonephric) duct
Reproductive.a: becomes female internal structures = Fallopian tubes, uterus, upper portion of vagina. o Wolffian (mesonephric) duct = becomes male internal structures = SEED = Seminiferous tubules, Epididymis, Ejaculatory duct, Ductus def erens. o SRY gene on Y chromosome produces testis

Reproductive.q: “Do I need to know about all of the ligaments relating to the uterus/ovaries, etc.?” o Unfortunately, USMLE cares. But I’ll tell you exactly the HY points: o Suspensory ligament of ovary = connects lateral ovary to abdominal wall. § Contains ovarian vessels. § Ligation of ovarian vessels during oophorectomy risks injury to the ureter. o Ovarian ligament = connects medial ovary to uterus. o Round ligament of uterus = connects uterine horns to labia majora. § Uterine horns are the superol ateral parts of the uterus that connect to the Fallopian tubes. o Cardinal ligament = connects the lateral cervix to pelvic wall. § Contains uterine vessels. § Ligation of uterine vessels during hysterectomy risks injury to ureter. o Broad ligament = large ligamen t that connects uterus, Fallopian tubes, and ovaries to pelvic wall. § Contains the ovaries, Fallopian tubes, and round ligaments of uterus. o Parametrium of uterus = fat and connective tissue surrounding the uterus. § 2CK Obgyn form mentions embryo developing w ithin parametrium of the uterus;
Reproductive.a: ectopic pregnancy. So just be aware of this term.

Reproductive.a: presents as boggy uterus postpartum; Tx with uterine massage, followed by intra

Reproductive.a: increased risk of endometrial cancer. Never give tamoxifen to woman who has a uterus. Give raloxifene instead.

Reproductive.q: cycle and stays at this higher temp; why?

Reproductive.a: follow

Reproductive.q: 23F + 10 weeks’ gestat ion + nausea and vomiting for 4 weeks + lost 1.8kg; what is the most likely adverse effect on the fetus?
Reproductive.a: = “no significant adverse effect.”

Reproductive.q: How to Dx hyperemesis gravidarum (HG)?
Reproductive.a: = urinary ketones.

Reproductive.q: Biochemical disturbance in HG?
Reproductive.a: hypokalemic, hypochloremic, metabolic alkalosis (low K, low Cl, high bicarb); yes, they ask thi s on Obgyn shelf.

Reproductive.q: Important drug causing hyperprolactinemia apart from antipsychotics?
Reproductive.a: metoclopramide = D2 antagonist.

Reproductive.a: decreased GnRH pulsation (hypogonadotropic) = decreased LH + FSH; Q wants “ ¯ FHS, ¯ estrogen” as the answer; in contrast, premature ovarian failure, Turner syndrome, and menopause have “ FHS, ¯ estrogen” as the answer.

Reproductive.a: fat necrosis (can calcify).

Reproductive.q: 44F + painless unilateral cyst in breast that drains brown serous fluid; Dx?
Reproductive.a: answer on Surg form 6 = fibrocystic change; everyone says wtf because, yes, classic p resentation is bilateral breast tenderness in woman 20s

Reproductive.q: 25F + sh arp pain in outer quadrant of right breast + exam shows 2cm tender area in right breast but no mass found; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = fibrocystic change.

Reproductive.q: co lored fluid + mass still present after aspiration; next best step?
Reproductive.a: = biopsy of the mass.

Reproductive.q: “alendronate now”
Reproductive.a: give bisphosphonate to patients commencing steroids indefinitely, or to patients receiving steroids frequently.

Reproductive.q: 45F + unilateral rusty nipple discharge; Dx?
Reproductive.a: intraductal papilloma until proven otherwise.

Reproductive.q: 45F + unilateral rusty nipple discharge + biopsy shows stellate m orphology; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = invasive ductal carcinoma, not intraductal papilloma.

Reproductive.q: outer quadrant; next best step?
Reproductive.a: = needle

Reproductive.q: 45F + inverted nipple + greenish discharge; Dx?
Reproductive.a: mammary ductal ectasia (widening of lactiferous duct).

Reproductive.q: 42F + recurrent miscarriage + SLE; Dx?
Reproductive.a: antiphospholipid syndrome (lupus anticoagulant) = Obgyn shelf will ask for “uteroplacental insufficiency” as the answer = Tx with aspirin or heparin; warfarin is contraindicated in pregnancy (bone abnormalities + bleeding in fetus).

Reproductive.q: 45F + SLE + commencing third course of corticosteroids during past 18 months; Q asks what else she should be given;
Reproductive.a: “alendronate now” = give bisphosphonate to patients commencing steroids indefinitely, or to patients receiving steroids frequently.

Reproductive.q: Which fetal parameter most reflective of IUGR?
Reproductive.a: a bdominal circumference; sounds wrong, as you’d expect perhaps femur length, or biparietal diameter, etc., but answer is abdominal circumference.

Reproductive.q: 23F + 33 weeks’ gestation + FVL mutation + intrauterine female demise; Q asks which vessel the thrombosis most likely occurred in;
Reproductive.a: uteroplacental artery.

Reproductive.q: Female at 24 weeks’ gestation + HTN + proteinuria; most likely cause for her findings?
Reproductive.a: = “uteroplacental insufficiency” or “placental dysfunction”; this is the cause of preeclampsia.

Reproductive.q: Female at 1 6 weeks’ gestation + HTN + proteinuria + fundal height measured at the umbilicus; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = hydatidiform mole, not preeclampsia; preeclampsia will occur after 20 weeks’ gestation ; molar pregnancy presents large for gestational age = fundal height at umbilicus is normally reflective of 20 weeks’ gestation .

Reproductive.q: Uteroplacental insufficiency can cause what issue on the fetal heart tracing?
Reproductive.a: = late decelerations (fetal hypoxia).

Reproductive.q: What do early, variable, and late decels mean?
Reproductive.a: early = fetal head compression; variable = cord compression; late = fetal hypoxia.

Reproductive.q: 160), however there’s zero variability; Dx?
Reproductive.a: answer on Obgyn NBME = fetal sleep state.

Reproductive.q: Fetus has HR at 180bpm, however there’s zero variability; Dx?
Reproductive.a: answer on Obgyn NBME = maternal fever.

Reproductive.q: What are accelerations?
Reproductive.a: fetal well

Reproductive.q: What is a biophysical profile?
Reproductive.a: assesses fetal wellbeing; often done when non

Reproductive.q: 21F + 41 weeks’ gestation + 4cm dilated + variable decels; next best step?
Reproductive.a: answer on Obygn NBME = amni oinfusion (wrong answers were external cephalic version, forceps delivery, amniocentesis, cordocentesis) = can’t attempt delivery if not 10cm dilated + forceps not tried first anyway because it can cause nerve damage or sternocleidomastoid trauma (vacuum e xtraction / suction cup delivery first).

Reproductive.q: What is external cephalic version?
Reproductive.a: transabdominal manipulation of a breech fetus into cephalic engagement; only performed after 36 weeks, as the fetus can spontaneously engage cephalically prior.

Reproductive.q: What is internal podalic version?
Reproductive.a: reorienting fetus within the womb during a breech delivery; may be attempted for transverse and oblique lies when C

Reproductive.q: old neonate + purplish fluctuant mound on scalp + crosses suture lines; Dx?
Reproductive.a: caput succedaneum

Reproductive.q: like eruptions within abdominal striae; Dx + Tx?
Reproductive.a: = pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy (PUPPP); occurs in ~1/200 pregnancies (usually primigravid); cause is unknown, presents as pruritic hives

Reproductive.q: 25F + G1P0 + third trimester + itchy palms + soles; Dx + Tx?
Reproductive.a: = intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP); usually occurs third trimester; pruritis, particularly of palms + s oles; diagnosis is achieved by ordering serum bile acids (elevated); Tx = ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol); important to note that ICP is associated with increased risk of third

Reproductive.q: day Hx of nausea and generalized itching + bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL + ALT/AST/ALP all normal; Dx?
Reproductive.a: Obgyn shelf = intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy; no mention of palms + soles itching in vignette.

Reproductive.q: 36F + G1P0 + 36 weeks’ gestation + nausea/vomiting + jaundice + high bilirubin + high ALT and AST + no mention of pruritis of palms/soles; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = acute fatty liver of pregnancy; caused by deficiency of long

Reproductive.q: 29F + G1P0 + 2 nd or 3 rd trimester + intensily itchy eruption around umbilicus that spreads outward; Dx + Tx?
Reproductive.a: = herpes gestationis (gestational pemphigoid); not HSV, but instead an idiopathic autoimmune phenomenon; Tx = topical steroids.

Reproductive.q: 13F + never had menstrual period + morning nausea/vomiting + suprapubic fullness; next best step?
Reproductive.a: = beta

Reproductive.q: Tx for HTN emergencies in pregnancy?
Reproductive.a: just know hydralazine can be used for this purpose.

Reproductive.q: Complete vs partial mole?
Reproductive.a: complete mole = karyotype of 46; empty egg fertilized by a sperm that duplicates; bunches of grapes / snowstorm appearance on USS; chance of progression to chori ocarcinoma higher than partial; partial mole = karyotype of 69; fetal parts visible on USS; lesser chance of progression to choriocarcinoma.

Reproductive.q: Anovulation + hirsutis m + BMI 27; Dx?
Reproductive.a: PCOS .

Reproductive.q: Anovulation ; mechanism USMLE wants?
Reproductive.a: insulin resistance = causes abn ormal GnRH pulsation = high LH/FSH = LH high enough to precipitate ovulation but follicle not yet adequately primed = no ovulation (anovulation) = follicle retained as cyst .

Reproductive.q: 32F + unable to conceive for 3 years + BMI 30 + acanthosis nigricans; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = T2DM (PCOS or anovulation not listed as answers; wrong answer is “hypercortisolism”) = Q doesn’t mention any characteristic features such as purple striae, muscle wasting, or central obesity.

Reproductive.q: 40F + vasomotor Sx; which hormone to confirm Dx?
Reproductive.a: = high FSH for premature ovarian failure.

Reproductive.q: 28F + Hashimoto th yroiditis + hot flashes for 6 months + high FSH; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = “autoimmune ovarian failure”; this is a cause of premature ovarian failure (autoimmune diseases go together).

Reproductive.q: Thyroid and pregnancy?
Reproductive.a: TSH normal, T3 normal, free T4 normal, total T4 elevated = due to increased thyroid

Reproductive.q: What do we order to evaluate thyroid function in pregnancy?
Reproductive.a: always choose free T4 if you are asked. TSH is for screening in non

Reproductive.q: Levothyroxine dose in pregnancy for those with Hashimoto?
Reproductive.a: may need to be increased up to 50%.

Reproductive.q: Thionamides in pregnancy?
Reproductive.a: methimazole is teratogenic in first trimester (causes aplasia cutis congenita); give PTU in first trimester; 2 nd trimester onward switch to methimazole (PTU significantly hepatotoxic + methimazole only teratogenic early in pregnancy).

Reproductive.q: 27F + 34 weeks’ gest ation + thyroid storm; Tx?
Reproductive.a: Obgyn NBME = PTU.

Reproductive.q: tender + TSH high + T4 low; most likely explanation for these findings?
Reproductive.a: = “thyroiditis” = Dx = postpartum thyroiditis (a type of silent thyroiditis ) = characterized by thyrotoxicosis followed by hypothyroidism (1/3 of women experience both phases; 1/3 experience ju st hyperthyroid phase; 1/3 only hypothyroid phase); affects 5

Reproductive.q: Neonate born with cretinism; what could have prevented this?
Reproductive.a: = “routine newborn screening”; yes, on obgyn shelf.

Reproductive.q: 16F + anterior vaginal wall pain and dysuria for 6 months + U/A normal + vitals normal; Dx?
Reproductive.a: chronic interstitial cystitis = Tx is supportive; do not choose ster oids.

Reproductive.q: Important factoids about acute appendicitis in pregnancy?
Reproductive.a: can be upper right quadrant; if appendicitis, yes, perform laparascopic appendectomy.

Reproductive.q: hCG hundreds of thousands; Dx?
Reproductive.a: choriocarcinoma (brain mets); chorio loves to metastasize to lungs.

Reproductive.q: 24F + pregnancy visualized in the corneum of the uterus; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = ectopic pregnancy.

Reproductive.q: 27F + pregnancy visualized in the parametrium of the uterus; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = ectopic pregnancy.

Reproductive.q: Most common location for ectopic?
Reproductive.a: ampulla of fallopian tubes.

Reproductive.q: Most common etiology for ectopic?
Reproductive.a: Hx of PID = scarring of fallopian tubes.

Reproductive.q: Tx for ectopic pregn ancy?
Reproductive.a: laparoscopic removal (salpingostomy / salpingectomy).

Reproductive.q: When to give methotrexate to Tx ectopic?
Reproductive.a: all must be fulfilled: beta

Reproductive.q: Org anisms causing PID + Tx?
Reproductive.a: chlamydia and/or gonorrhea; Tx = IM ceftriaxone, PLUS either oral azithromycin or oral doxycycline. If patient is septic (2+ SIRS), = admit to hospital and give IV antibiotic therapy (they make this distinction on Obgyn sh elf).

Reproductive.q: PID + fever does not improve after several days on Abx; next best step?
Reproductive.a: adnexal USS to look for tubo

Reproductive.q: Difference between inevitable and threatened abortions?
Reproductive.a: inevitable = bleeding + open cervix; threatened = bleeding + closed cervix; Tx for inevitable = vacuum aspiration; Tx for threatened = bed rest.

Reproductive.q: 32F + 9 weeks’ gestation + bleeding and passage of clots per vaginum + intrauterine pregnancy seen on USS; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = incomplete abortion (passage of clot s means it’s already underway).

Reproductive.q: Difference between complete and missed abortions?
Reproductive.a: Complete = no products of conception seen on USS (abortion is literally over/complete); missed = fetal demise without passage of products of conception.

Reproductive.q: “third measurement of beta - hCG within one week”
Reproductive.a: Dx here is spontaneous abortio n; must measure beta

Reproductive.q: 43F + bleeding per vaginum + uterus is large and smooth; Q asks for which type of uterine fibroid;
Reproductive.a: submucosal leiomyomata.

Reproductive.q: 43F + no bleeding per vaginum + uterus is globular; which type of fibroid?
Reproductive.a: = subserosal.

Reproductive.q: 43F + beefy red mass protruding from the vagina; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = pedunculated submucosal leiomyomata uteri, not cervical cancer = the latter will often be desc ribed as an ulcerated, exophytic mass.

Reproductive.q: 42F + comes in for routine exam + no complaints + large uterus on exam + USS shows various leiomyomata; next best step?
Reproductive.a: = observation (because asymptomatic); otherwise Tx = NSAIDs, OCPs.

Reproductive.q: 44F + dysmenorrhea + menorrhagia + USS shows large, smooth uterus with no overt masses; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = adenomyosis (endometrium growing within myometrium); may present similar to su bmucosal fibroids, with vaginal bleeding, however uterus is diffusely enlarged and no masses seen on USS; Tx with NSAIDs, OCPs; leuprolide; definitive is hysterectomy.

Reproductive.q: 27F + 30 weeks’ gestation + weakness of thumb abduction bilaterally; Dx?
Reproductive.a: carpal tunnel syndrome (normal in pregnancy).

Reproductive.q: 23F + unintended pregnancy + fever of 104F + vaginal discharge + abdo pain + laceration visualized on cervix; Dx?
Reproductive.a: septic abortion = she tried to self

Reproductive.q: 32F + rupture of membranes (ROM) >18 hours + abdo pain + fever; Dx + Tx?
Reproductive.a: chorioamnionitis; Tx = ampicillin + gentamicin + clindamycin (amp + gent alone seen as answer on one Obgyn shelf Q).

Reproductive.q: section 12 hours ago + abdo pain + fever; Dx + Tx?
Reproductive.a: postpartum endometritis; Tx = ampicillin + ge ntamicin + clindamycin.

Reproductive.q: Organism(s) causing chorioamnionitis + endometritis?
Reproductive.a: = polymicrobial.

Reproductive.q: 25F + postpartum endometritis + low BP; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = puerperal sepsis; gynecologic infection starting 1

Reproductive.q: Lu mp seen at 4 or 8 o’clock position on vulva; Dx + Tx?
Reproductive.a: Bartholin gland cyst/abscess; Tx = warm compresses for cyst; drain if abscess.

Reproductive.q: Organism(s) causing Bartholin gland abscess?
Reproductive.a: = polymicrobial.

Reproductive.q: “most serio us complication of this condition?”
Reproductive.a: answer = necrotizing fasciitis; wrong answer =

Reproductive.q: 37F + Bartholin gland abscess + Q asks “most serio us complication of this condition?”
Reproductive.a: = necrotizing fasciitis; wrong = “gram positive sepsis” (polymicrobial; need not be gram +).

Reproductive.q: Grey/whitish patchy/rough area on the vulva or perineum; Dx + Tx?
Reproductive.a: lichen sclerosus = must do punch biopsy fir st to rule out SCC; if confirmed LS, do topical steroids; if SCC, surgically excise.

Reproductive.q: SCC of perineum in diabetic; biggest risk factor in this patient?
Reproductive.a: = HPV, not dysglycemia.

Reproductive.q: 15 mL of serosanguinous fluid aspirated from the cul de sac; Dx?
Reproductive.a: ruptured cyst (usually corpus luteal); Tx = supportive.

Reproductive.q: 24F + Hx of ovarian cyst + colicky pelvic pain past few weeks + pain has become constant past couple days + 6x8cm palpable adnexal mass; Dx?
Reproductive.a: ovarian/adnexal torsion (cyst is a risk factor).

Reproductive.q: 24F + Hx of ovarian cyst + intermittent pelvic pain for four hours that has become constant past two hours + 8x10cm palpable ad nexal mass; Dx?
Reproductive.a: ovarian/adnexal torsion (pain may be weeks or hours).

Reproductive.q: 24F + increasingly severe pelvic pain the past couple days + 6x8cm mass palpable in the adnexa; Dx?
Reproductive.a: torsion.

Reproductive.q: 25F + normal periods + LMP 20 days ago + 5cm mobile mass in right adnexa on examination + slightly tender to palpation; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst; wrong answer is endometrioma (chocolate cyst seen in endometriosis).

Reproductive.q: 18F + tampon use + diffuse rash + BP 90/60; Dx?
Reproductive.a: toxic shock syndrome ( S.aureus ).

Reproductive.q: 24F + 30 weeks’ gestation + spotting on underwear 12 hours after sexual intercourse + bleeding gradually increasing since + USS normal; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = cervical trauma.

Reproductive.q: 36F + 26 weeks’ gestation + severe flank pain + feels faint when attempting to urinate; Dx?
Reproductive.a: uro lithiasis (progesterone slows ureteral peristalsis).

Reproductive.q: Mechanism for increased cholesterol gallstones in pregnancy?
Reproductive.a: progesterone slows biliary peristalsis + estrogen increased activity of HMG

Reproductive.q: trimester miscarriages + has single kidney; Q asks most likely reason for recurrent miscarriage;
Reproductive.a: congenital uterine abnormalities.

Reproductive.q: hCG neg ative + USS shows simple 5cm cyst; Tx?
Reproductive.a: = “oral contraceptive therapy and a second pelvic examination in 6 weeks”; the wrong answer is “reassurance and schedule follow

Reproductive.q: 23F + extremely painful periods + needs to miss grad school classes sometimes because of the pain + examination shows no abnormalities; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = primary dysmenorrhea = “prostaglandin production” = PGF2alpha hypersecretion.

Reproductive.q: Above 23F; next best step in Mx?
Reproductive.a: = NSAIDs; pregnancy test is wrong answer.

Reproductive.q: 23F + extremely painful periods + needs to miss grad school classes sometimes because of the pain + examination shows nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = endometriosis. Obgyn shelf will often omit details such as pain with defecation or dyspareunia because they’re too easy.

Reproductive.q: How to Dx endometriosis?
Reproductive.a: = diagnostic laparoscopy.

Reproductive.q: 26F + dull pelvic pain + USS shows cystic mass with calcification; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = dermoid cyst (mature cyst ic teratoma); details such as “hair, skin, teeth” are too easy for Obgyn shelf.

Reproductive.q: 65F + multiple masses “caked” on the omentum; Dx?
Reproductive.a: ovarian cancer.

Reproductive.q: 31F with epilepsy + 10 weeks’ gestation + has seizure + phenytoin serum level below therapeutic range; next best step?
Reproductive.a: = increase dose of phenytoin (yes, during pregnancy) = seizure leads to fetal hypoxia, which is worse case scenario, so must prevent at all costs.

Reproductive.q: 31F on valproic acid wanting to get pregnant; what do we do?
Reproductive.a: stop valproic acid (contra indicated in pregnancy due to high chance of neural tube defects) = can use other anti

Reproductive.q: 52F + hot flashes + urge incontinence; Q asks mechanism;
Reproductive.a: “estrogen deficiency.”

Reproductive.q: “hypoestrogenic state”
Reproductive.a: Tx = lubricants; if insufficient, topical estr ogen may be used.

Reproductive.q: “recommendation for use of a lubricant”
Reproductive.a: high prolactin levels during breastfeeding à hy poestrogenic state à Sx similar to atrophic vaginitis in menopause.

Reproductive.q: replacement therapy (HRT)?
Reproductive.a: severe vasomotor Sx (hot flushes, urge incontinence); HRT is not used for preserving bone density; increases risk of thromboembolic and cerebrovascular events; estrogen increases fibrinogen and factor VIII levels.

Reproductive.q: 57F + blo od stains on underwear for 6 months + painful sexual intercourse + atrophic, friable vaginal mucosa on exam + cervix and bimanual exams normal; Dx + Tx?
Reproductive.a: atrophic vaginitis = = “hypoestrogenic state” = Tx = lubricants; if insufficient, topical estr ogen may be used.

Reproductive.q: 25F + currently breastfeeding + menstruation not yet resumed + dyspareunia + erythematous vagina with no discharge; next best step in Mx?
Reproductive.a: = “recommendation for use of a lubricant” = high prolactin levels during breastfeeding = hy poestrogenic state = Sx similar to atrophic vaginitis in menopause.

Reproductive.q: HRT increases the risk of what kind of cancer?
Reproductive.a: = breast, not endometrial; greater absolute amount of estrogen over female’s life increases breast cancer risk; HRT does not increas e endometrial cancer risk; latter is unopposed estrogen as risk factor, which is why HRT is estrogen + progesterone; only time HRT is given as estrogen only is for women with Hx of hysterectomy.

Reproductive.q: 53F + taking HRT past six months + stopped taking progesteron e component because she didn’t like how it affected her moods + vaginal bleeding; next best step?
Reproductive.a: answer on Obgyn shelf = endometrial biopsy.

Reproductive.q: palpation; next best step?
Reproductive.a: = FNA biopsy of the cyst.

Reproductive.q: “ACTH hypersecretion”
Reproductive.a: in congenital adrenal hyperplasia caused by 21

Reproductive.q: 16F + aunt died of ovarian cancer + asks GP how to screen for ovarian cancer; what is your response?
Reproductive.a: = no screening, but offer her information about oral contraceptive pills.

Reproductive.q: degree family members with gynecologic cancers; next best step?
Reproductive.a: = total abdominal hysterectomy and bil ateral salpingo

Reproductive.q: oophorectomy performed for leiomyomata uteri; Q asks what we do re Pap smears;
Reproductive.a: “no longer indicated.”

Reproductive.q: 22F + T1DM + 33 weeks’ gestation + fundal height 38cm; Dx?
Reproductive.a: polyhydramnios (fundal height in cm should approximately = # of weeks pregnant).

Reproductive.q: Neonatal girl with karyotype 46XX + has phallus and scrotum; Q asks mechanism;
Reproductive.a: “ACTH hypersecretion” = in congenital adrenal hyperplasia caused by 21

Reproductive.q: 33F + prenatal USS shows two f etuses with thick dividing membrane; what kind of twin pregnancy is this?
Reproductive.a: = dichorionic diamniotic; thick dividing membrane = two chorions; # of placentae = # of chorions.

Reproductive.q: 33F + prenatal USS shows one fetus much larger than the other; what kind of twin pregnancy is this?
Reproductive.a: most likely to be monochorionic monoamnionic in the setting of twin

Reproductive.q: hCG as part of IVF protocol + develops severe abdo pain + ascites; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome = almost always due to iatrogenic beta

Reproductive.q: 21F + requests OCPs + Pap smear is normal; Q asks what else needs to be done;
Reproductive.a: check for chlamydia = should be noted that whilst Pap smears always start at 21, STI checks are done from age of sexual onset.

Reproductive.q: 33F + regular periods + Hx of multiple sexual partners + unable to conceive with husband for 3 years + husband has normal semen sample; next best step?
Reproductive.a: = hysterosalpingogram (assess tubal patency and uterine architecture; possible Hx of PID leading to tubal occlusion (despite no Hx of ectopic in the patient).

Reproductive.q: 35F + hysterosalpingogram shows spillage of dye into the peritoneal cavity; Dx?
Reproductive.a: normal finding (fallopian tubes are normally open at both ends).

Reproductive.q: What is uterine didelphys?
Reproductive.a: uterus develops as paired organ (double uterus) + double cervi x +/

Reproductive.q: 52F + presents for routine screening for first time in 4 years; Q asks “in addition to cholesterol screening, Pap smear, and mammography; what does she need?
Reproductive.a: = colonoscopy. Similar answers might be influenza vaccine if fall/wi nter (every year).

Reproductive.q: How often are Pap smears indicated, and when are they started and stopped?
Reproductive.a: commenced at age 21, then every 3 years; starting age 30, can become every 5 years if co

Reproductive.q: Mx of LSIL on Pap smear?
Reproductive.a: if negative HPV testing, repeat co

Reproductive.q: grade squamous intraepithelial neop lasia (HSIL) on Pap smear?
Reproductive.a: regardless of HPV status: immediate loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP), OR colposcopy + biopsy.

Reproductive.q: 57F + vaginal hysterectomy performed for CIN III; next best step?
Reproductive.a: Obgyn shelf = “Pap smear annually.”

Reproductive.q: 32F + colposcopy is performed for LSIL + entire squamocolumnar junction cannot be visualized; next best step?
Reproductive.a: answer on Obgyn NBME = cone biopsy.

Reproductive.q: 47F + Pap smear shows atypical glandular cells + colposcopy normal + endocervical curettage shows benign cells; next best step?
Reproductive.a: Obgyn NBME = endometrial biopsy.

Reproductive.q: 35F + two minutes after separation of placenta has shortness of breath + tachy cardia + bleeding from venipuncture sites; Dx?
Reproductive.a: amniotic fluid embolism; can cause DIC; supportive care.

Reproductive.q: section + gets up to go to the bathroom + SoB + tachycardia; Dx?
Reproductive.a: pulmonary embolism = heparin followed by spiral CT (if not p regnant) or V/Q scan (if pregnant).

Reproductive.q: 39F + pregnant + Sx of pulmonary embolism + V/Q scan performed showing segmental defects; next best step in Dx?
Reproductive.a: = spiral CT; student says “wait but I thought we don’t do CT in pregnancy.” Right, we don’t. But if they ask for next best step after V/Q scan, that’s still the answer they want.

Reproductive.q: section + temp 100.8F + breath sounds decreased at both lung bases + urinary catheter specimen is negative + remainder of exam unremarkable; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = atelectasis (most common cause of fever within 24 hours of surgery (but shelf has two days after C

Reproductive.q: trimester painless bleeding + ROM + fetal bradycardia; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = vasa previa (fetal vessels overlying the in ternal cervical os); associated with velamentous cord insertion (vessels not protected by Wharton jelly).

Reproductive.q: tapering vessel extending to margin of membranes; Dx?
Reproductive.a: a nswer = succenturiate placental lobe; students says wtf? = just need to know sometimes placenta can have auxiliary lobe with connecting vessels; this is a cause of vasa previa, in addition to velamentous cord insertion.

Reproductive.q: section 6 weeks ago + required 3 units of transfused RBCs + 9kg weight loss + has cold intolerance + could not breastfeed; Dx?
Reproductive.a: Sheehan syndrome (arrow Q on shelf; answer is ¯ for prolactin, ACTH, GH, FSH, TSH); should be noted tangentially that o n newer NBME for Step 1, Q with Sheehan syndrome has for aldosterone (not hyperaldosteronism, but higher baseline to compensate for lower cortisol).

Reproductive.q: month Hx of intermitten t pelvic pain + BP of 90/50 + bluish bulge in upper vagina; Dx?
Reproductive.a: hematometra = imperforate hymen with blood collection in the uterus = vagal response causes low BP = Tx = cruciate incision of the hymen.

Reproductive.q: month Hx of intermittent pelvic pain + BP normal + bluish bulge in upper vagina; Dx?
Reproductive.a: hematocolpos = blood

Reproductive.q: 27F + delivered newborn 5 days ago + pain in calf with dorsiflexion of foot; next best step in Dx?
Reproductive.a: = duplex ultrasonography of the calf; positive Homan sign for DVT in hypercoagulable state.

Reproductive.q: Most common cause of abnormal AFP measurement?
Reproductive.a: = dating error.

Reproductive.q: 32F + protrusion of distal urethra through urethral meatus; Dx?
Reproductive.a: urethral prolapse; sounds reasonable, but don’t confuse with stress incontinence; the latter will sometimes be described as “downward mobility of vesicourethral junction with Valsalva” (not urethral prolapse).

Reproductive.q: 22F + 24 weeks’ gestation + fundal height 20c m + no cervix palpated + examination shows fetus in breech position in vagina; Dx?
Reproductive.a: cervical incompetence; Tx w/ cervical cerclage; notable risk factor is prior conization.

Reproductive.q: 30F + 37 weeks’ gestation + fetus in breech position; during labor, risk of which complication is greatest?
Reproductive.a: = cord prolapse.

Reproductive.q: 32F + 14 weeks’ gestation + Hx of two LEEP + cervix flush against upper vagina and measures 2cm in diameter + pelvic USS shows funneled lower uterine segment; Dx?
Reproductive.a: cervical incompetence = “funnel” means cervical incompetence (“cervical funneling” / “funneled lower uterine segment”).

Reproductive.q: 87F + partial prolapse of uterine cervix through the introitus + uterus can easily be pushed back into the uterus; next best step?
Reproductive.a: = vaginal pessary.

Reproductive.q: What is definition of protracted latent phase?
Reproductive.a: dilating <1

Reproductive.q: What does “arrest of active phase” mean?
Reproductive.a: no cervical change in >4 hours despite adequate con tractions (>200 Montevideo unites [MVU]), or >6 hours if contractions inadequate.

Reproductive.q: 28F + 38 weeks’ gestation + cervix completely dilated + strong contractions + fetal station remains unchanged over next hour; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = cephalopelvic disproportion (baby too big for pelvis).

Reproductive.q: smelling yellow vaginal discharge + blood spotting on underpants + no dysuria + mild vulvar erythema seen on exam; Dx?
Reproductive.a: = vaginal foreign body, not sexual abuse; presumably sexual abuse there would be lacerations or trauma seen on physica l exam.

Respiratory.q: What do I need to know about FEV1/FVC?
Respiratory.a: normal ratio is considered >0.7 (according to AAFP); ratio is decreased in obstructive lung disease (<0.7; <70%); ratio is normal or increased in restrictive lung disease (>0.7; >70%) . In both obstructive and restrictive, FEV1 and FVC, as independent variables, both decrease; it’s o nly the ratio that differs.
